speechtext:

In light of the negotiations in progress in Quebec between fluid milk producers and industrial milk producers and given the fact that their differences will probably not be ironed out for a few weeks; considering that the Canadian Dairy Commission has arbitrarily decided not to pay subsidies to the milk producers of Quebec as long as both opposing groups will not

That the House urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to direct the Canadian Dairy Commission to issue not later than April 1 the cheques which the milk producers of Quebec are entitled to and which should never be issued later than necessary because of protracted negotiations or legal hassles.

speechtext:

Pearson when he was in office, that no commitment of peacekeeping forces shall be made without the approval of this House by affirmative resolution. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, pursuant to Standing Order 43. In light of the fact that volunteer firefighters risk life and limb at all hours of the day and night to provide fire protection and emergency services for in excess of 2,500 communities in all provinces and territories, and in light of the fact that towns and municipalities provide compensation to volunteer firemen for their donation of time and personal expense, while the Government of Canada allows them only $300 maximum for tax exemption purposes, which does not cover costs and acts as a disincentive to serve, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):
That this House acknowledge that due to inflation, the federal government deduction of $300 per year under the Income Tax Act is grossly inadequate and, further, that the allowable annual deduction for costs incurred by these community-minded volunteers be raised to the level of $1,000 per year.

speechtext:

Also, $100 million was the amount of credit for the creation of jobs-the bill was passed and became effective in February- and there was the $1.6 billion which was approved under Bill C-ll, voted at the end of December. speechtext:
The reason I preempt the time of the House to do this now is because it will relate to some interest members will have relative to possible enrollment dates at universities. I thought I should take a moment to explain this to members, because during the recess information will be going out about it. I thought hon. members ought to be the first to know.

Since coming here it has been an interest of mine, and many others have shared it and many others had it long before that time, that we find a way to encourage young Canadians to participate in the House of Commons by serving as pages here. That was attempted at the high school level and faced great difficulty because of discrepancies and differences in various academic programs throughout the provinces.
A couple of years ago I asked the Clerk of the House of Commons to attend in Washington to examine the system there. He did, and returned with a very thorough report which was referred to the Members' Services Committee. The members of that committee worked very diligently on the project, with great interest, and came up with what I think is an excellent idea. I hope all members will share it. It is that the program, instead of being operative at the high school level, be operative at the first year university level, which facilitates provincial interchange much more easily and enables residents away from home to lead a much more normal course of life.
Having given approval to that basic idea, we are attempting now in some hurry to implement, at least partially, this program before September, which will involve possible enrollment by students in two Ottawa universities, whose co-operation we have received throughout and for which we are very grateful.
1 want to assure hon. members on a couple of counts. First, this program will be phased in in such a way as to ensure that all of those who have served so faithfully and well as pages will not in any way be prejudiced or jeopardized in the employment they have enjoyed here.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege of which I gave Your Honour the required notice under Standing Order 17(2). My point of privilege relates to certain things that have been happening and may still be happening to my friend and colleague, the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth). I have indicated to you, sir, the nature of the matter, and I have also discussed it with the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo).
Some time ago, back on February 13, a letter was written to the hon. member for Northwest Territories by the president of the 1978 Arctic Winter Games Host Society which read as follows:
Dear Mr. Firth:
The 1978 Arctic Winter Games will be held in Hay River and Pine Point from March 19 to 25, 1978. The games will be officially opened by Mrs. Iona Campagnolo, Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport, at 2 p.m., in Hay River, on March 19, 1978.
We would be most pleased to have you come to Hay River for the Opening Ceremonies, and to participate in the various activities at Hay River and Pine Point.
We would appreciate your early advice on this matter in order that we might make the necessary arrangements with respect to accommodation.
Yours very truly
D. M. Stewart
On February 27 my friend and colleague replied to Mr. Stewart's letter in these words:
Dear Mr. Stewart:
I would like to thank you for your kind invitation to be part of the Opening Ceremonies and to participate in the various activities at the 1978 Arctic Winter Games, to be held in Hay River and Pine Point from March 19 to 25.
I would be more than pleased to attend and should be arriving in Hay River on March 18.
With kindest regards
Sincerely yours,
Wally Firth, M.P.
Northwest Territories
Privilege-Mr. Stanley Knowles
That is where my hon. friend is today. Someone might ask whether this matter should not stand until he returns, but in my view when an affront is offered to one member of this House it is an affront to all of us.
I feel there has been an affront, and a certain amount of intimidation which I regard as rather serious. The invitation was quite clear. The hon. member for Northwest Territories was to take part in the activities connected with the Arctic Winter Games, particularly the opening ceremony at Hay River on Sunday, March 19, at 2 p.m. However, after that invitation had been extended and accepted there were certain telephone calls.
My information is that it was either Mr. Stewart himself, the Mayor of Hay River, who is also an official connected with the games, or someone from his office who telephoned to the office in this building of the hon. member for Northwest Territories and also to the office of my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). A complaint was made that the hon. member for Northwest Territories would apparently be attending the Northwest Territories NDP nominating convention which would be held in Hay River during the time the Arctic Winter Games were taking place. What is wrong with that, I do not know.
Of greater concern to me than the affront to the hon. member is what seems to me to be intimidation with respect to the election process itself. This, indeed, is the serious matter which I raise. The information given by Mr. Stewart or his office to the office of my hon. friend and to the office of my leader was that unless the nominating convention were cancelled, his invitation to take part in the opening ceremonies and to participate in activities connected with the games would be cancelled.

subsubtopic: MR. KNOWLES (WINNIPEG NORTH CENTRE)-ARCTIC WINTER GAMES-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE IN ELECTORAL NOMINATING PROCESS
speechtext:
My friends in the Progressive Conservative party are trying to put the blame on the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport. My hon. friend from the Northwest Territories does not do that. He thinks she is on his side and that it is the local people, in charge of a project funded by government money, who are snubbing him and, what is worse, interfering with the election process.
I do not mind snubbing. I can take it. We all get it now and then. It is part of our occupation; our skin is not that thin. But when an invitation is rescinded and everyone else is invited, and when an hon. member who represents the largest constituency in Canada is not invited to a ceremony in his own constituency, it becomes an affront which I am sure the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport will not condone. In fact, I suspect she will be the first to extend an apology to the hon. member for Northwest Territories when he returns.
What I think is really serious is that local people who are operating a function which is largely, if not wholly, funded by federal money, should use their position to intimidate a person or group of persons in connection with the election process. At that point it becomes a matter of privilege as far as this House is concerned.
I suppose it may be said that the New Democratic Party in the Northwest Territories is taking advantage of the fact that many people have come in from all over that vast area and decided that it would be a good time to hold a convention. I think this makes good sense. It probably means saving money, because people might make the trip only once, rather than twice. And to suggest that a convention held in the basement of a motel in Hay River would interfere with the carrying on of the Arctic Winter Games is utter nonsense.
On the other side of the coin, persons like Mr. Stewart, who is president of the Arctic Winter Games Host Society and Mayor of Hay River, by taking these various steps to interfere with the election process are probably infringing the Canada Elections Act itself and this, consequently, is a case of privilege as far as hon. members here are concerned.
The things which have happened are too many for this to be accidental. There was the written invitation. It was not just one of those printed cards which might go to anyone. It was a personal letter. There was an acceptance. Then there was the telephone call saying that unless this convention was postponed the invitation would be rescinded. There were calls not only to the hon. member's office in this building but also to the office of the leader of this party. Then there is the fact that the name was omitted from the list of those attending the opening Sunday afternoon. There is the fact that there was no invitation to attend the reception held by the government of the Northwest Territories on Monday night. As I say, these things add up to an attempt to dissuade a member of this House from pursuing his rightful privilege of being a candidate for nomination for the next parliament.
I felt this matter should be raised without further delay. Obviously, Your Honour would not want to rule until the hon. member himself has returned from the games, and I hope he will be re-nominated tonight. Your Honour would want to look into this, as would the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport), perhaps the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner), and perhaps also the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen), who is in charge of the Canada Elections Act. However, I decry in the strongest terms this kind of interference on the part of local officials. Your Honour might, under normal circumstances, tell me to complain to those officials up there, but the fact is they are operating a function which is funded by the federal government.
I decry, in the strongest terms I can use, these practices which interfere with the rights of any citizen but particularly with the right of a member of this House of Commons to seek re-nomination so that he can return to this House. It is a matter which is the cause of a great deal of concern in the north. I have had read to me some of the things that are appearing in the newspapers. There is a feeling that there was an element of discrimination against the hon. member in his own person for certain reasons which I need not state, and I think the matter should be cleared up.

March 22, 1978

I am a little sorry that my friends to my right seem to think that the blame should be put on hon. members opposite. I do not want to blame the hon. minister opposite. I want her help. The hon. member for Northwest Territories says the minister was most kind to him when she spoke to him Sunday afternoon after the event was over, and I am sure she would not condone what has happened, but I hope somehow this matter can be sorted out and, if the time comes when Your Honour feels that either I or the hon. member for Northwest Territories has a prima facie case of privilege, either he or I will be prepared to make the necessary motion to refer to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections the specific matter of certain officials interfering with the election process.

speakeroldname: Hon. Iona Campagnolo (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subsubtopic: MR. KNOWLES (WINNIPEG NORTH CENTRE)-ARCTIC WINTER GAMES-ALLEGED INTERFERENCE IN ELECTORAL NOMINATING PROCESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the chief magistrate of one of the host cities of the Arctic Winter Games has certain privileges in the administration of his city, but I do not believe it is our purpose to determine the scope of those administrative duties here.
I would like to note that there are two separate matters at issue in the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and I thank him for giving me the information he did at the beginning of the question period. The first is the alleged lack of recognition by the games organizers of the presence of the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) at the opening ceremonies. The second point, I believe, is whether it was appropriate for the hon. member for Northwest Territories to use the assembly, for which all travel costs had been paid by the people of Canada, as an occasion at which to hold his nominating meeting for the next federal election in the Mackenzie constituency.
On the first point I would like to point out that there was a great deal of informality at the opening ceremonies of these games. The dais was crowded with honoured guests. Indeed, it was overcrowded with honoured guests, many of whom were not accorded public recognition in other than general terms.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned, I in fact did see the hon. member for Northwest Territories immediately after the ceremonies concluded. He was taking pictures from the front part of the dais, as he had moved himself from the seat he had, closer to the second row. The hon. member approached me, and I told him that if I had known he was there I would have recognized him in my preamble, as I certainly would have. However, I would like to note that there was no introduction of guests on the program. There was a spoken program. A man was acting as M.C.
Also on the platform was the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Milne), and he was not introduced either. I am sure that the parliamentary secretary was not being intimidated because he intended to have his nominating meeting for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe as part of the opening of the Arctic Winter Games.
On the second point, which I feel is the more important point, the propriety or lack of it with regard to using the
Privilege-Mr. Stanley Knowles
Arctic Winter Games as a vehicle for a collective meeting of northerners for a nomination meeting, I can only say that hon. members opposite have frequently said to me that they wish to see less involvement of politics in sport.
I am absolutely not in a position to comment on what was said between the mayor of Hay River and the hon. member for Northwest Territories. I have no way of establishing what was said in that conversation or if, indeed, it took place, as I am quite sure the hon. member will tell me when he returns. What one individual says to another is quite beyond the realm of purview of my ministry. However, just before making this statement I confirmed that the hon. member for Northwest Territories was and is a fully accredited official of the Arctic Winter Games. In addition, the Arctic Winter Games organizing committee has the hon. member registered as a V.I.P. of the society, which, I understand, grants him automatic inclusion in all events.
I regret very much that any slur might be cast upon the Arctic Winter Games, and I know that is not the intention of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The Arctic Winter Games is the largest event of this type in the world above the 60th parallel, and since more than 600 athletes from Alaska, Yukon, and the Northwest Territories, organizers and volunteers, are all involved, I do not believe any of them should suffer because of the politicization of superb hospitality and fellowship for which these games are famous. I regret that the hon. member for Northwest Territories feels that a discourtesy has been done him, and I hope that we may look forward to the next Arctic Winter Games in 1980 in Whitehorse without any such charges of political opportunism being levelled.

Mr. Edward Broad bent (Oshawa-Whitby): Mr. Speaker, I would like to address myself to two questions that have been raised during the question of privilege. I must say that I was quite disappointed in the minister's response to what I thought was a very courteous and generous presentation of the issue by the House leader of my party.
The issue raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in terms of holding a convention for any political party in Canada was that there should not be any kind of intimidation by any local group in this country, particularly a local group that has been federally funded, and that could inhibit that process. The local group concerned, if I understand it correctly, was appointed by the minister who spoke on the issue, intimidated-and I will use it openly-the member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth), who happens to be, and it has not been mentioned, a Metis in this country. For that reason, he happens to be a little more sensitive maybe than the rest of us when he is subjected to what most of us could call a put-down by the white majority.
I think it is useful for us to discuss this issue, but not so naively as to assume that a minority feel just the same as the rest of us when they are confronted by such a situation. The hon. member for the Northwest Territories, in my view, very appropriately, in terms of the interests of the people he represents in that part of Canada, decided to have a political convention. It is true that he chose a time when a lot of people were coming in for another function, and it is true that they were going to be using public funds for that convention. 1 would like to point out to the minister that most of these people might not have been able to come the hundreds of miles to a political convention if such had not been the case.
The minister, who sort of oozed her way around the point that perhaps the hon. member for the Northwest Territories was inappropriately having a convention at that time, was incorrect. It was quite the contrary. I would like to see all of the political parties-and I am not making a criticism of the other parties-seize such opportunities, in a part of the country where most people are too damned poor to attend a political convention. Rather than seeing it as a fault, Mr. Speaker, I see it as a virtue.
The member for the Northwest Territories-and let us not be naive about that either-is going to get the nomination. He has done a good job, and there is no local opposition to him for the nomination. All he wanted to do was take advantage of the event and schedule the convention when it was going to be open to a lot of people who are in the main poor and spread over hundreds and thousands of miles. What happened was that a local official, for God knows what reason, but certainly not a good reason, attempted to intimidate that member and

said, "No, you can't have this convention at this time or we are going to strike you off from the official list of participants in the opening of these important games."
I say that is wrong. There was nothing wrong with the scheduling of that meeting. I repeat, I would be happy if all the political parties of Canada could schedule their meetings at a time when people could attend. Once again, it was poor people in the main. I resent the minister getting up, and instead of replying with some courtesy to what I took to be a courteous and generous comment by the House leader of my party and, indeed, courteous comments of the member for the Northwest Territories himself, implying that it was inappropriate for him to have a convention at that time. That kind of suggestion on her part, to put it euphemistically, was less than gracious.
I do not want to take up the time of the House. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre stated, it is a ruling that you will have to make, Mr. Speaker, and it should probably be left over to a later date when the hon. member is back in this House. I wanted to make the comments that 1 did today because, instead of responding in an appropriate way, the minister who entered into the debate did just the opposite. Explain.

Mr. Speaker, I can explain this bill very briefly. Its purpose is to standardize the time for federal elections in this country so that a general election would be held every four years on the third Monday of June. In the event that a government loses the confidence of parliament, then an election would be held immediately, and thus parliamentary democracy would be preserved. The present system during majority parliaments turns election dates into protracted guessing games that disrupt the normal flow of business both within and without parliament. The selection of the election date ought not to be at the political whim of the Prime Minister, but should be fixed in law for the good of the country.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to my motion No. 3, which is on the Order Paper today, 1 think 1 should start perhaps by making the observation that when Bill C-25, to establish an agency to oversee the construction of the northern pipeline, passes the House of Commons and work gets under way, this project will likely be the largest and most important ever undertaken by private enterprise in the history of the world.
Canadians in all parts of the country support very strongly the creation of a northern pipeline. They recognize that as well as having tremendous benefits to Canada in terms of ensuring that in future we will have adequate supplies of energy for Canadian needs, it will also have industrial spin-offs in all parts of Canada and will have enormous benefits in terms of business in the country, trade, and badly needed jobs. No Canadians more than Ontarians and Quebecers support the construction of the pipeline. They recognize that their interests as Canadians and as members of particular provinces lie very directly with the creation of the pipeline itself.
The central point which I hope to make in moving the motion I have proposed is that the government appears to be bulling ahead in setting up an agency to oversee the construction of the northern pipeline without having provided for input from the provinces in all parts of the country.
Under clause 17 of the bill a federal-provincial consultative council is to be created which would have responsibility for carrying out the objects of Bill C-25. It would consist of the Commissioner and a representative of the Yukon Territory, named by the governor in council upon the recommendation of the Commissioner and Council of the Yukon Territory, and one representative of each of the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, and Saskatchewan, nominated by the lieu-tentant governors in council of each of those provinces.

March 22, 1978
Northern Pipeline
Perhaps it would be worth while to take a short bit of the time of the House to go back and review the objects of the bill as listed on pages 2 and 3. The three very important objects are these, and I would remind hon. member that I stress the fact that the objects are national in scope. They do not simply affect one part of Canada, but affect the development and future security of energy supply for all of Canada. Object (d) is:
(d)	to facilitate, in relation to the pipeline, consultation and co-ordination with the governments of the provinces, the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories;
It does not say just the western provinces, it says "the provinces", meaning all the provinces.
Object (e) states:
(e)	to maximize the social and economic benefits from the construction and operation of the pipeline including the maximizing of the opportunities for employment of Canadians while at the same time minimizing any adverse effect on the social and environmental conditions of the areas most directly affected by the pipeline;
Again, although there are some areas of the country that will be affected more than others, no one part of the country is excluded from this object of the bill.
Object (0 does not refer to provincial, northern or western. Object (f) states:
(f)	to advance national economic and energy interests and to maximize related industrial benefits by ensuring the highest possible degree of Canadian participation in all aspects of the planning and construction of, and procurement for, the pipeline while ensuring that the procurement of goods and services for the pipeline will be on generally competitive terms.
Earlier today during the question period we heard comments by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) which amounted to an attack on the Premier of Ontario because of a letter he sent to the Prime Minister of Canada asking that he get under way in taking action on those proposals agreed upon by the provinces and the federal government to get the economy back on track. 1 believe the comments today, which were very unconstructive on the part of the Minister of Finance and will do nothing to help Canadians who today are unemployed, gave a very graphic example of this government's attitude toward co-operative federalism.
If we have problems in Canada today, for example the question of national unity, in large part the blame must be shouldered by the national government, by this government, because of its failure to consult with all the provinces and to share power with the provinces in determining what the national priorities will be for the development of Canada. If this government were serious about wanting to promote and foster national unity, and about building a strong, united, and harmonious country, it should show by example that it is prepared to open the doors and invite co-operation of the type from all levels of government.
It was with this intent in mind, of sharing in the decisionmaking process, and having the opportunity of input in the decisions which will affect the citizens of this province, that the Ontario Energy Minister, Mr. Reuben Baetz, came to Ottawa on March 14 to appear before the Special Committee on the Northern Gas Pipeline.

At that time Mr. Baetz argued very strongly about this federal-provincial consultative council being set up by the government to ensure that the objectives included in this bill are recognized and achieved properly. He argued that the government of Ontario and the citizens of this province ought to have their voices heard. I think the case made by the Ontario Minister of Energy was a compelling one.
That minister pointed out that Ontario is by far the largest market for natural gas in Canada; about 50 per cent of all the natural gas used in Canada today is consumed by Ontarians. He pointed out that, by far, Ontario is the largest potential market for gas from the Mackenzie Valley and Prudhoe Bay, particularly if a gas swap takes place. That is obvious as it would involve the transmission of gas to southern Ontario through the entire length of the pipeline. Ontario is also the largest producer of the goods and services which will be used in construction of the pipeline. Clearly Ontario has an interest in having some say in the policies which are set up and which will determine what sort of pipeline will be created.
The province and the people of Quebec, while not so immediately concerned with the pipeline project as are the citizens and the province of Ontario, will also be affected in the same way by decisions which will be made. The motion I propose is not simply to include a representative of the province of Ontario on this consultative mechanism, but also to include representatives of the other major consuming province, Quebec. The opportunity is here today for government members to show that they are concerned about the impact this pipeline will have on the citizens of these provinces, and to allow them to have some say in its development.
The province of Ontario has followed the pipeline hearings very closely and has been represented at many applications before the National Energy Board. Ontario was also represented on several occasions before the Mackenzie pipeline inquiry. Ontario is not requesting, and we should stress this, to be placed at the centre of the pipeline decision-making, but merely wants to be consulted and allowed to present alternative proposals on matters which very substantially touch it.
Liberal members on the committee see this federal-provincial consultative council as being responsible for the co-ordination of the pipeline in those areas where it is to be built. Unfortunately, I was out of the country on official business and was not able to be present at the committee meetings, but I have studied the transcript closely. If I understand their position correctly, government members of the committee see the bill in question as not being concerned with the pricing of gas for the Ontario and Quebec markets because this matter would go before the National Energy Board, but as being concerned with the construction of the pipeline. They also feel that if the Dempster lateral is built, a new regulatory agency might be set up for that project. Other members of the government feel that the government would successfully protect Ontario's interests. For some incongruous reason they feel that while the government is well eauipped to protect the
March 22, 1978

interests of the consuming provinces, it is necessary to set up a federal-provincial consultative mechanism to ensure that the interests of the territories, British Columbia, Alberta, and Saskatchewan, were protected. Why is the federal government in a position to protect the interests of the consuming provinces but not of the other provinces? That was not explained.
If the pipeline is to be built for the benefit of all Canadians, according to clause 3 of the bill, we have to recognize that consultation should not only take place in those parts of the country where the pipeline is to be built, but the provinces that are to consume the gas should also be heard. The fact that decisions on pricing may be taken later by the National Energy Board does not alter the fact that the way the pipeline is built will largely affect the final price. Ontario and Quebec have a real interest in seeing how this pipeline is to be built.
I do not intend to go on at great length, Mr. Speaker, but I think it is worth while to put on record an editorial which appeared in yesterday's Ottawa Citizen. Members of the government will recognize that this newspaper is not known as supporting this party, but traditionally supports the government. The editorial deals with the presentation made to the committee by the Minister of Energy for Ontario, which is the position I am trying to take today on behalf of the people of Ontario and Quebec. The editorial has a headline, "Why Not a Seat for Ontario?" and reads as follows:
Is it so unreasonable for Ontario, this country's biggest consumer of natural gas, to have a seat on a federal-provincial pipeline council?
Ontario Energy Minister Reuben Baetz thinks not, and his argument makes sense.
But he's having trouble convincing the Commons pipeline committee. Liberal MPs argue that because the federal government will look after the interests of the country as a whole, that committee's membership logically should be limited to representatives from the areas through which the pipeline will pass.
These areas-the Yukon, British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan- don't seem to feel that way. Alberta has already told Baetz to apply for membership and the others have indicated they support his bid.
Let me stress this again, Mr. Speaker. The other provinces which are to be members of the federal-provincial consultative body, support the proposal made by Ontario. The only opposition comes from this government in this House.
The editorial continues:
Ontario is neither trying to cash in on a major western project, nor step on federal jurisdiction.
This province, from its experiences with Syncrude and Polar Gas, merely wants to ensure that "the Canadian portion of the northern pipeline (be) constructed in the most economic manner."
All in the interests of what Baetz calls "co-operative federalism." Nothing sinister in that.
I think this editorial makes good sense, Mr. Speaker. It is up to members of the government to explain why they oppose allowing people in the consuming provinces to have a say in decisions which will very dramatically affect the level of industrial development in this part of Canada and also the cost of energy to Ontario consumers. I believe that if the government today is willing to be flexible, this can be a step forward for federal provincial consultations and for co-operative federalism.
Northern Pipeline
I must say I was disappointed to read the comments of one Liberal member, in the committee transcript. The fact that he is a Quebec member is irrelevant and does not bear on this. The fact that any member of the federal parliament should make such a gratuitous attack on another province can only be a blow to federalism. In the proceedings of the Special Committee on a Northern Gas Pipeline of March 14, 1978, the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Dawson) is reported as follows:
As far as co-operative federalism is concerned, I would not want to be very critical but I do not think co-operative federalism means Ontario, Ontario, and Ontario. I think it has to be more than that. 1 do not think Ontario should be involved whether it is the construction of a pipeline in western Canada or of a Quebec and Maritime pipeline perhaps being built in the province of Quebec in future years.
This sort of statement coming today with national conditions in Canada being what they are, can only serve to polarize Canadians and to drive a wedge between the provinces. I think it is important that members of this parliament, members of the Canadian government, prove that they are prepared to recognize the right of all Canadians in every part of Canada to have a say in decisions which will affect their lives and the economy.
I hope that members of the government who are present today will review the motion I have placed on the order paper.
I hope that they will search their consciences and ask themselves what their constituents would want them to do-whether they feel that their constituents believe that the consuming provinces have a right to be heard in decisions which will affect them? I hope they will agree to allow this very sensible amendment to go forth with the support of all sides of this House.

Northern Pipeline

As I stated in my first amendment, I hope that we will get 90 per cent or more of the contract work and jobs that the government has been promising but is unwilling to commit itself to in black and white in the legislation before us. It seems to me important in view of the eventual amount of steel of steel to be used, if the Dempster lateral is built, that Ontario have a voice in this Council which is dealing with these matters, because of its interest.
I commend to the House the motion moved by the hon. member. I think it makes sense. I do not understand this government's reluctance to involve the province of Ontario. I think there is some similarity with the Syncrude project. We have had joint federal-provincial involvement in energy projects like this in the past. Mr. Speaker, I am not sure that I support the substance of this motion, in fact I suspect I would be against it, but I do rise to support its procedural admissibility. I always enjoy coming to the defence procedurally of something I may not agree with, but that is the position I take.
Northern Pipeline
First of all, I should like to point out that when Mr. Speaker was giving us his preliminary review of all the proposed report stage amendments he did not raise any question about motion No. 7. This was not for want of his looking at the procedural aspects of the motions because he did question motion No. 2, and in due course ruled it out or order.
I followed the arguments put forward by the parliamentary secretary and I appreciate his point; indeed, I respect it. But it seems to me that what we have here is a motion in itself that corresponds to the situation of a private member seeking to move the reduction of a tax. That, I emphasize, Mr. Speaker, is permitted. A member cannot move for an increase in taxation, but on a number of occasions members have been allowed to move for a reduction in a proposed tax. When that has been done, members on the government side have argued that it upsets the balance of ways and means, that if the government loses money that it wants from one source it would have to make it up somewhere else. I have been around here long enough to remember when that argument carried some weight. But starting about 20 years ago it was discredited, it was argued that the phrase "balance of ways and means" really meant nothing even though the reduction in a tax might force the government to find the money somewhere else, it was still competent for a private member, without a Governor General's recommendation, to move a reduction in a tax.
What we are talking about here is a fee, tax, or cost that a private company would have to pay. The hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Bawden) is seeking to impose a limit on how much that private company might have to pay. In the interests of procedural consistency and in the interest of applying the same rule today that we apply when there are proposals to reduce taxation, the Speaker's original hunch that No. 7 was not out of order should be confirmed today.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Drummond (Mr. Pinard) has supported extremely well the arguments that I have made in the figures that he quoted in his remarks a few minutes ago. Yesterday I sought the advice of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who has spoken on this question in a technical sense today. I will not cover that again.
The hon. member for Drummond stated that in his research he found that the Alyeska pipeline, which ran for some 800 miles, had cost the federal authorities in Alaska an amount of some $7 million. He then quoted the much longer length of the Foothills pipeline and made an exact comparison. The hon. member has related a cost of $70 million that was spent by their regulatory agency, the successor to the Federal Power Commission now known as the Federal Energy Resources Commission.
As I recall, the Alyeskan pipeline cost something between $7 billion and $8 billion. Therefore the 1 per cent formula that I have proposed would present a more conservative estimate of cost if we applied the same percentage of the total cost of the pipeline as we find that the costs of the regulatory agency in Alaska cost that agency in comparison with the total cost of other pipelines.
It is important to recognize that the Alaska pipeline planning costs started out at a very early time after oil was discovered on the north slope. It was extended for many years. It was shut down. It was held up for all kinds of technical reasons and environmental reasons. The fact is it stretched out over probably three or four times as long a construction period as would have been the case if it had been pursued expeditiously.
It is interesting to note that the Alaska pipeline was constructed to a large extent above ground. It carries oil, not gas.

It offers many more serious problems in traversing perma frost. A lot of the pipeline is elevated rather than buried.
In summary, I was pleased to have the hon. member confirm to me that a 1 per cent formula to limit the costs of government expenditures in this project will be completely consistent and somewhat more conservative than was the case in Alaska where so many more difficulties were encountered.
Clause 29 of Bill C-25 states that the pipeline will pay the cost, not only of the regulatory agency that is proposed, but also of other government departments that have inputs and charges to this agency over a period of time as their activities relate to the northern pipeline. In other words, all of the costs that are chargeable as they relate to the pipeline are to be passed on to the Foothills Pipe Lines Limited. This is acceptable. However, these costs that are passed on should be within reason.
It is for this reason that I have proposed this amendment. I am convinced, by everything I have seen over a number of years as they relate to government departments, that these things can and likely will get seriously out of hand. If no upper limit is placed, we are in effect giving the government a blank cheque as it relates to its expenditures. I am sure all Canadians would be concerned about giving this government a blank cheque, particularly those connected with the Foothills Pipe Lines Limited.
A limit such as I am proposing could easily be a vital matter when it comes to financing. As we hear about the difficulties that are to be expected and the problems of the Foothills Company, one of their greatest problems and difficulties will be arranging the financing. If the Foothills Pipe Lines Limited can make their estimate of some $4 billion for a massive project like this, surely the government can give some estimate of what its costs are going to be.
The people who will be principally involved in the financing of this, in the final analysis are going to be the large institutions which carry the debt. It is important when we are passing this bill to recognize that limits-

Order, please. 1 wonder if 1 could *sk the indulgence of the hon. member for just a moment. It seems the clearest way to get at the procedural aspects of this motion is to ask the hon. member to give some indication. The import of his amendment is to put a ceiling on costs passed along to the pipeline. It is unclear to me whether the effect of the amendment is to put a ceiling on the costs themselves or simply to put a ceiling on those costs that are passed by the public treasury to the pipeline company.
If indeed it does not control the total cost, but only that portion which is passed along to the pipeline company, the effect of the amendment could be to leave the residue of cost as a charge on the public treasury. If, however, the effect of the amendment is to control the cost in the total and thereby limit the amounts that are passed along, it would seem there is not a procedural problem; it is an amendment the merits of

which would be decided upon the floor of the House. All I want to hear from the hon. member is whether the effect would be to control the entire cost or simply that portion which is passed on to the pipeline, leaving the residue to be picked up by the taxpayer, in which case the amendment would require an amendment to the royal recommendation.

speechtext:
1 cannot be certain how the government or the pipeline agency will behave. If they know there is such a limitation in the legislation it might very well be they would work within the cost limitation proposed by the amendment. If, on the other hand, they chose, perhaps recklessly, to exceed this limitation, the cost would be carried by the public treasury. But it would depend entirely upon the activities and planning of the pipeline agency.
I feel it is important to bear in mind that this precedent will apply in the future to other massive energy projects. It could relate to pipelines in the southern part of Canada. Because of this it is important, in my view, that we do not allow the government an open-ended opportunity to spend money.
In relation to the point which Your Honour has made, I should like to make it clear that this formula would be much more generous if the pipeline were to be built in the southern part of one of our provinces or were related to other projects where similar government supervision was required. If, for instance, the agency proposed to overrun the expenditure limit suggested in my amendment, the money could easily be recovered from savings on future pipelines which might run through less difficult terrain. Over a period of time, the averaging principle would apply. As to the question of whether the government is likely to exceed this limit or not, I stress once again that the limit proposed is greater than in the case of the Alyeska pipeline and five times as great as the limit the Federal Resources Commission utilized in the United States.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, it is a very fine distinction which has to be made here. Your Honour has expressed the view that if there is a risk that the amendment might impose a charge on the treasury it would be out of order. With great respect, I submit there must be clear evidence that a charge would be imposed on the public treasury before an amendment ought to be ruled out of order on such grounds.
The amendment before us could be further amended. One per cent amounts to $40 million. The amendment could be amended by the imposition of a 10 per cent limitation, and no one in his right mind would expect the government to impose a $400 million ceiling. As the hon. member has just told us, $40 million is five times the amount the United States has mentioned in its legislation on a similar matter and it is far greater than in the case of the Alyeska pipeline which was desperately mismanaged. There is no reason whatever why the $40 million ceiling suggested should be exceeded. Indeed, the argument put forward by the hon. member for Calgary South would, hopefully, persuade most hon. members that the cost to the government with respect to the agency and the plethora of
Northern Pipeline
other charges to be incurred will amount to much less than the one per cent limit suggested by the amendment.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the discussion in the standing committee on this matter I raised some objection to this proposed motion, both on the ground that it did probably impose a charge on the public and also because I did not think a percentage of this kind, if it were realistic, would be anything but a floor under expenditure. I propose to deal only with the first of these arguments since it touches the question Your Honour has raised.
It seems to me this proposal is only important if it does actually put forward a limitation. So when the hon. member for Yukon says it could be amended to 10 per cent, he does not mean it seriously. It would have no purpose at all, then. The whole purpose is to restrict in some way a charge upon the company. If it is to be a restriction it could very well result in an additional cost over and above the amount payable by the company. This would fall upon the Government of Canada and thus the proposed amendment would require a message which recommended such additional expenditure.
I might add that if the hon. gentleman intended this to be a real restriction he could have amended his proposal very easily by saying, "provided that such costs shall not exceed one per cent" and by adding the words "that would be the cost imposed upon the company."

the discussion today has given me a much clearer understanding of the implications of the amendment of the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Bawden). It raises a very difficult procedural problem because there is not the absolutely clear necessity of a charge upon the treasury which would usually enable the Chair to set the motion aside.
I now understand fully the intention of the hon. member for Calgary South. It is a measure of fiscal control on the operation, and therefore he is saying in his argument that what he is doing is not using this amendment in such a way as simply to limit that amount of money which is to be passed on to the pipeline by the government but rather is forewarning the government that, in providing the services that are required by the statute, it will suffer a limitation in the amount of money it can spend in respect to those services and pass on to the pipeline company, and therefore saying to the government that it does not have an open-ended cost recovery mechanism, and a blank cheque, as it were, to provide these services.
At first it appeared to me that that reasoning was sound and that the amendment could be allowed on procedural grounds. As I examine it, though, I am afraid that what it amounts to is this: In the first place, in addressing himself to the financial provisions that are contained here, His Excellency would be examining a statute which would be setting up a regime in which the government would be required to provide certain regulatory services at a cost which would not be subject to a limit, and that cost would be passed along to the private company and to the private sector by virtue of this section, and therefore would be no charge on the treasury.
The imposition of a limit, it seems to me, sets up either the possibility that the cost of providing these services would exceed the limit, in which case there would be a charge on the treasury which His Excellency could not have envisaged in giving his recommendation or, alternatively, the possibility that the government might have to come, in providing the services that are required of it in the statute, to a position in which it says, "These regulatory agencies that we are required . to provide in this statute must be discontinued because we foresee that we have achieved the ceiling and, by virtue of this amendment, we cannot spend any more money. Therefore, we will have to take the regulatory agencies out of business".
I think that on the one hand the result of the hon. member's amendment would be a charge on the treasury. On the other hand, the one I have just described is surely a concept which is foreign to the statute as it now exists. If it is going to be introduced, it would have to be introduced in some other way because it seems to me to go beyond, in that respect, the scope of the statute as it was originally envisaged, and therefore it seems to me that on either one or the other procedural ground I have just cited, the amendment will have to be struck down.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the intent of motion No. 4 standing in my name is to amend the pipeline bill so that we can be assured that the rights and interests of the native people of the Yukon will be upheld by parliament if a pipeline is to go through territory which would affect them in terms of their land claims. The intent of the amendment is to ensure that pipeline construction would not proceed on a section upon which a native land claim settlement has not yet been negotiated. As many hon. members realize, the situation in the Yukon is fraught with difficulty as far as relationships between native and non-native people are concerned.
There is hope among the majority of Yukoners that the Alcan pipeline will bring economic benefit in the form of new business, and the creation of jobs for local residents, and that it will do so in such a way as to provide economic benefit without significant economic damage. This is a concern I share with those who reside in the Yukon Territory.
Yukoners do not have to look very far to see the damaging economic and social effects that accompanied the construction of the Alyeska oil pipeline in the state of Alaska. There they saw tremendous price increases as hundreds of people moved into the area and land became scarce, which drove prices up and affected accommodation, goods, services and wage rates.
Northern Pipeline
Prices escalated to the point where many people employed in normal businesses or in municipal or state governments left their jobs for jobs related to pipeline construction. As a result, many essential services in the communities of Alaska suffered. There is fear among Yukoners that a similar situation might arise, and unless we have very strict monitoring of the pipeline, many people will face inflation that may get out of control.
Many people-and I think of public servants whose wages are going to be held down by this government-may find themselves falling further behind as inflation escalates in the general economy due to pipeline activity. The pipeline could be a blessing or it could be a disadvantage for Yukoners. In that kind of economic milieu, one must also be cognizant of the social impact of the pipeline, not only on the white or nonnative community, but on the native community as well. Again, one need only look at the situation in Alaska to realize the social upheaval that occurred in that state during the construction of that pipeline which was of a negative nature as far as native people were concerned. With the influx of many white workers from the south and their different value systems and attitudes, the native people saw what was left of their traditional always and social patterns challenged.
In looking at the Yukon Territory, we must recognize-the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) will agree-that there is a great difference between the needs and situations of the native people in the Yukon and those indigenous people, the Inuit and the native people, of the Northwest Territories.
Mr. Justice Berger addressed himself to the social and economic implications of the proposed Mackenzie Valley pipeline for the indigenous people of the Northwest Territories. It was a thorough and exhaustive report which captured the imagination of northern and southern residents. Mr. Justice Berger stated in his report that the way we went about constructing a northern pipeline would tell us more about ourselves than anything else. It would tell us, who are the majority living south of 60, what we really believe to be the rights of those people living in the far north. It would tell us whether we put our own economic gains, through receiving energy from the north and jobs from construction, above the rights and interests of the people who have to live there after the pipeline has been constructed and the transient workers have moved on.
Mr. Justice Berger indicated that we have to accept and acknowledge the rights of the minority groups living north of 60. It is to the principle outlined in the exhaustive studies of Mr. Justice Berger and to a lesser extent the studies of Dean Lysyk that my amendment is addressed. We have to respect the rights of minorities in this country. Anyone committed to the principle of majority rule must acknowledge the other fundamental principle of a democracy, minority rights.
In the history of our country the acknowledgment of minority rights as they pertain to native people has been a very sad chapter. I need not catalogue the lists of broken promises and broken treaties that non-natives have perpetrated on the native people, who believed that when we signed something and when

we said we believed in the rule of law and justice we should be taken at our word, only to find later that the white man spoke with a forked tongue. More recently, the history of this Liberal government only confirms the suspicions of the native people that they will get a raw deal when there are only verbal assurances. Indeed, even when there have been written treaties or written guarantees, they have been broken.
As a parliamentarian, I can only hope for the best. In my view the best is to have something that is the law of the land enshrined in an act of parliament which will hold this government responsible for its provisions. The bill we have before us on the northern pipeline has in it no mention of native land claims or native rights. This is an essential matter that must be settled before the pipeline can proceed. 1 cannot foresee Foothills being able to go to the money markets of the world to raise the necessary capital for this pipeline unless the issue of native land claims has been settled. When I see no provision in the bill for settlement of these claims, I become very suspicious. Surely, to have my amendment accepted would put some pressure on the government to settle native land claims expeditiously and fairly.
Negotiations on native land claims in the Yukon Territory began in a serious way in 1973. Here we are in 1978 with only minimum progress having been achieved. We require some type of measure to force the government to stop dragging its feet on the matter of native land claims.
Surely we need to put some pressure on the government, through a legislative amendment, in order for it to get down to business and to recognize that the land claims must be settled fairly before the pipeline can proceed. If that amendment is contained in the legislation, then there is the pressure of law and the pressure of the company to get these claims settled as well. Because we have that amendment in law, hopefully it will ensure a just settlement, and not have native people settling with a gun held to their heads. I understand that is the fear of many of the native people of the Yukon Territory: unless there is a hard provision in this bill, they will be sacrificed to the expediency of getting the pipeline constructed.
In this regard I should like to refer to the testimony of the chairman of the Council for Yukon Indians, when he appeared before the Lysyk inquiry, which was studying the issue of native land claims and environmental problems in the north. Before that inquiry, the chairman said the following:
A pipeline now would mean a substantial influx of white immigration both as a direct and indirect result of the project. We would become an even smaller minority in our own land. We would have no land and no resources. We would have almost no political influence and decisions would be made by the vast white majority which would control our lives. We would not have had time to develop our own structures of decisions making and we would have no land or resources to make decisions about. We would be relegated to the political backwaters of our own land. We would remain an underdeveloped people with no prospect for improvement. Our constitutional and aboriginal claims to self-determination would be effectively lost.
It would turn the land claims negotiations into an elaborate, although perhaps dramatic, farce, with our people relegated to playing a few bit parts in the scripts.

That was the fear expressed by the Council of Yukon Indians. I believe it is still the fear of that group today.
We have received assurances from the president of Foothills indicating that he would not proceed to build a pipeline through that territory without the people in the affected region agreeing to it. I should like to refer to his policies and undertakings recorded in the transcription of his appearance before the National Energy Board. In particular I refer to the December 10, 1976, transcription under the heading: "Settlement of Land Claims and Public Acceptance of the Project". Mr. S. R. Blair stated the following:
Foothills has taken the position that construction of a pipeline in Yukon should not proceed until there is a broad acceptance of the project by the residents of that area.
Of course that is open to interpretation. How does one define broad acceptance? Is that 10, 20, 50 or 60 per cent of the people? Approximately 20 to 30 per cent of the residents of the Yukon are of native origin. They are not an insignificant minority. Surely if the president of Foothills has given an undertaking that he will not proceed unless there is a broad acceptance on the part of the residents of the area, then the amendment which I have put forward is not unreasonable in terms of the opinion of the company itself.
One factor of the Foothills application which impressed Canadians, over that of the Mackenzie Valley one by Arctic Gas, was the commitment of the company to listen to the people of the area and to take account of their needs. Thus, in light of that testimony, I think my amendment would be acceptable to the company, given Mr. Blair's commitment to the people of the area.
Now, the government has undertaken preliminary negotiations. A planning council has been set up. This planning council is a government agency which was set up to negotiate with the native people. This was an attempt as expediting the negotiations. The planning council indicated that the goals of a settlement were as follows:
Restore, protect, preserve and guarantee the identity of Yukon Indians and their freedom to choose a way of life in harmony with their cultural heritage.
Provide land and other forms of compensation to the Yukon Indian people to compensate them for loss of lands traditionally used and given up under the settlement so that they may have the opportunity to build an economic base equal with that of other Yukon citizens.
Provide the Yukon Indian people with the incentive and opportunity to have their rightful say, within the context of a one-government structure, in the decisionmaking authority which governs their everyday life.
That is a commitment of goals on the part of a government negotiating committee. I submit these goals are perfectly consistent with the amendment I am proposing today.
The native people in the Yukon Territory are not as dependent on land and the migratory hunting way of life as the people in the Northwest Territories and the Mackenzie Valley. Native people have been assimilated more into the white economy in society in the Yukon. Indeed, some native people have undertaken economic ventures in mining and what-have-you. That is to their credit. But a great sense of commitment to the land by these people still exists, as well as a realization that traditionally the land has been their way of life. Their
March 22, 1978

rights to that land have never been extinguished by any treaty or similar provision. Therefore, if a pipeline is to go through that land, which has traditionally been theirs to live and hunt on, surely it is reasonable to expect some kind of compensation and some kind of formal arrangement as to what will remain their land and what will be ceded to the pipeline company. We require a formal arrangement regarding the settlement of native land claims.
I believe hon. members of the Conservative party, and particularly the official spokesman for Indian affairs, would have some sympathy with the amendments 1 propose. Construction of the pipeline through native lands, or lands claimed to be under native jurisdiction, should not proceed until a settlement regarding that land area has been negotiated. Indeed, I listened with interest to the hon. member for Lamb-ton-Kent (Mr. Holmes), the Conservative spokesman on Indian affairs, during the debate on the northern pipeline, when he was commenting on the Lysyk inquiry. He quoted from that inquiry as follows:
For the reasons stated in Part E of this chapter, some additional time is desirable to avoid prejudice to a just settlement. Construction of the pipeline should not commence before August 1, 1981.
That is quoted from the Lysyk inquiry. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent went on to say:
Dean Lysyk was not recommending a moratorium. He was not recommending some unrealistic time delay; his was a responsible position. He was recommending a responsible time in keeping with the complexities and sensitivity of the issue in the Yukon Territory. Yet this government chose to ignore this important recommendation.
Further on during that debate on February 15, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent stated, as reported at page 2899 of Hansard:
The government's game plan is obvious. With the passage of this legislation the momentum of the project will impede efforts to conclude a fair and just settlement. The rights of individuals can be conveniently shunted aside in the name of progress.
I share the fear expressed by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent that unless we have some strong provisions in the bill before us, the native people will be sacrificed to the expediency of getting this construction under way by 1981. Indeed, the government has advanced Dean Lysyk's recommendation, that construction not begin until August, 1981, to January, 1981.
1 think a fair and just native lands claim can be achieved by 1981, but only if this government begins to recognize that which it has failed to recognize so many times in the past, namely, the legitimate and just claims of the native people in the area. This government has dragged its feet in these negotiations. We need something in the legislation to prod it along, and make it realize that we will only accept a just settlement for the native people in that area.
I have looked as well at the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, which I understand the government will accept, regarding the issue of native land claims, and I fear it is not as strong as that hon. member would want, or as strong as I would like. It in effect says that if a land
Northern Pipeline
claim has not been settled by the time the pipeline is under construction through the affected territory, the pipeline will be allowed to continue to be constructed, but that will not jeopardize the future rights of the native people in the area to obtain a just land claim settlement.
Unfortunately, that is inadequate. The negotiating position of the native people is certainly weakened if that provision passes, because we will have a situation under which the pipeline in effect is in place, and therefore the negotiations in a sense will be after the fact.

Marie (Mr. Symes) as I feel he has given the House the impression that the government is not interested in expeditiously arriving at a settlement of the claims in the area that will be traversed by the pipeline. I have always felt that the fair and just settlement of land claims was one of the most important things we are doing, not only as a government, but as a country. And I am convinced that the fair and just settlement of the land claims north of 60 is a precondition to the sort of normal political economic evolution that everyone in the north would like to see take place.
The government is in a position to back up what it has said with concrete evidence of what it has done within the last year

Northern Pipeline
on the question of land claims. The government was a party to the James Bay settlement. That was a settlement which members opposite have attempted to portray as a sell-out of Indian and Inuit interests. To the contrary, an examination of that settlement will demonstrate to any fair minded person that it is a good if not better than any other settlement made anywhere in the world by a government of a country in which native peoples live. It is even better when you take into consideration the various social services that will continue to be supplied by the two senior governments. On the basis of that settlement it is necessary in the future that governments, provincial or federal, when tackling this question of land settlement claims, must recognize that they have to pay for any interference with the rights exercised by the native people in a given area, whether those rights are in respect of trapping, hunting, fishing or otherwise. The second important precedent was set by the James Bay agreement, which the NDP chose to ignore, and which the hon. member for the Northwest Territories particularly chose to ignore, which I find very strange, that is, it set a precedent for the settlement of claims with non-status Indians. their destiny than any other group of people in this country. They are optimistic. Mr. Speaker, I want to address myself to motion No. 6 which stands in my name. At the outset, however, I want to thank the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) for recognizing my interest in the problems of the native people. I am somewhat surprised that he did not share the same concern with respect to the native problem in British Columbia, specifically in the northeastern part of British Columbia, which is equally significant.
May I say to the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) that I think that he has not quite understood the James Bay settlement. I am sure he remembers very well the position this party took on that question. It was a very fundamental principle that this government would extinguish unilaterally the rights and signatories of third parties to that agreement. The hon. member knows very well that that is the position this party took, and knows very well that an amendment that I presented to this House on the very fundamental issue, to preserve the minority rights of one group, was defeated by the government.
I recognize that the government has accepted the motion in my name, but I think it is important to reflect for a moment or two on what has transpired within the last few weeks and few years. In my view, it will reflect upon the sensitivity of the government with respect to Indian and native problems. I must say that despite the rhetoric we have heard from the government and the various pious statements we heard from the hon. member for Laprairie referring to some of them, if one follows the proceedings very carefully one comes to the inescapable conclusion that native and Indian people are being sacrificed in the name of progress. I made reference to this in the previous debate.
When the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner) spoke on second reading, he attempted to emasculate the government's position on the second stage inquiry. The minister attempted to convey to this House that the issue of land claims was proceeding very smoothly and that there would be no problem in resolving that issue. I know any individual in this House or in committee who has followed the events carefully over a period of time recognizes that that position was unrealistic and untenable.
One only had to listen to or read the testimony given by the Council of Yukon Indians or the Union of B.C. Chiefs when they appeared before the committee to understand the depth of feeling and concern for the future.
My colleague from Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle), described the problem in north-east British Columbia and the way in which he hoped this government might move to
March 22, 1978

involve the native and Indian people of the area in the pipeline process.
When I spoke on second reading and at the committee hearings I raised several critical issues where, in my view, the government abrogated its responsibility in respect of the native and the Indian people. In doing so, it jeopardized the trust relationship between the native Indian people and the Government of Canada, and therefore seriously jeopardized the prospects for a fair and just settlement.
As 1 indicated, the government broke its promises with respect to a second stage inquiry. I have no intention of going into the details, Mr. Speaker, but you will recall that the Lysyk commission was formed and in a three-month period Dean Lysyk went to all the communities in the Yukon and indicated to the Indian and native people that there would be a second stage inquiry if the pipeline came through that area. Indeed, the former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development made that promise, not only to the Indian and native people of that area but to the people of Canada, that if a decision was made for a pipeline in that area there would be a second stage inquiry. In the fall of 1977 the Union of B.C. Chiefs, under the very able direction of George Manuel, requested that a second stage inquiry be carried out in the north-east part of British Columbia. Again, that was rejected by the government.
In my opinion, there are still no guarantees in this legislation vis-a-vis the socio-economic impact, Mr. Speaker. It was pointed out very clearly in testimony that when one is setting the terms and conditions for pipelines, the socio-economic problems must be identified early and set out in those terms and conditions. That is why it was essential to have a complete study of the socio-economic impact with respect to the Indian and native community.
Extreme difficulties had been encountered on the issue of land claims. On second reading I pointed out that the government had dragged its feet. Let me review quickly what has transpired. The Council of Yukon Indians presented their excellent document entitled "Together Today for our Children Tomorrow", in 1973. Shortly after that negotiations got under way, but initially the negotiators had no mandate from the federal government to carry out any specific or effective negotiations, and progress was painfully slow. The former minister went north to Whitehorse on March 3, 1975, and made a unilateral offer to the native people, breaking down the normal consultative process that the Indian and native people anticipated. Obviously it was rejected at that time.
Then, sir, in October, 1975, they appointed Digby Hunt as a negotiator for the federal government. He was well known to be one of the architects of the development of the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. We knew at the time he would be rejected by the Indian and native people in terms of negotiations, and yet this government undertook to appoint him as a negotiator. Obviously, once again, the negotiations failed. Then for about the third time, in 1977 negotiations commenced with Dr.
Northern Pipeline
Naysmith. I can remember the minister of Indian affairs of those days telling us in glowing terms about the progress and success that were being achieved in those negotiations.
In a press release the Council of Yukon Indians, who appeared in Ottawa just prior to the second reading debate, gave a statement. During second reading of this bill I quoted from this press release the following:
We are now faced with some clear choices. We can continue to oppose a pipeline until our land claims are settled and be labelled as radical and anti-development. Or, we can compromise, thereby, sacrificing our rights to self-determination on our home land.
We have decided not to compromise but to fight!
We will take our case to the Canadian people. We will demonstrate the humanity and justness of our position. We will use every legal means at our disposal to ensure that we achieve a fair and just settlement. On February 13th, the Federal Court will rule on our opposition to the National Energy Board recommendations. Our struggle to achieve self-determination will not stop there.
That, to me, is not a sign of negotiations proceeding smoothly with the federal government. The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie referred to it when I spoke on second reading. I made reference to the very significant recommendation of Dean Lysyk which I quoted at page 2898 of Hansard, February 15, 1978. It reads:
For the reasons stated in Part E of this chapter, some additional time is desirable to avoid prejudice to a just settlement. Construction of the pipeline should not commence before August 1, 1981.
Sir, one had to ask very serious questions at that time when the agreement between the United States and Canada was signed to commence construction of the pipeline in the Yukon on January 1, 1981. Why the difference? If the federal government had been truly interested in the Indian and native people in that area in the Yukon, surely it could have negotiated within the recommendations as outlined by Dean Lysyk. Obviously the federal government declined to do so.
Again, during the committee hearings we have the document which appeared at the pipeline committee hearing. Is there any wonder why the Indian and native people have distrust for this government, and why it is essential to have at least some sort of protection in this particular legislation? Let me quote from this document which appeared before the standing committee.
The Government of Canada is prepared to extinguish native land claims if necessary by legislation to support its international word and commitment but it will only do so in a way which represents the fairest possible settlement to those involved.
There is additional material here which, quite frankly, cannot help but impair the trust relationship between a government and the Indian and native people. It must be recognized, sir, that it was in this context and with this background of material and the knowledge we have had, for example, of the James Bay experience, which my good friend from Laprai-rie referred to a few moments ago, that we approached this bill in committee. Indeed, I want to point out there was nothing in the original legislation that made reference to the Indian and native people. Can you imagine, sir, there was nothing in the original legislation that made reference to the Indian and native people? tee on a Northern Gas Pipeline during the very first meeting I asked the very question of the Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council (Mr, MacEachen). Let me give you his answer to my question regarding the fact that no reference to the Indian and native people was in the legislation itself. It reads:
