I am not exactly clear whether I understand your question properly, but I gather you have in mind some reference in the legislation to the desirability or the necessity of assuring a just settlement of Indian land claims, and the recognition of their rights. We have given some thought to that and we would certainly be interested in hearing further views as to how we might give that recognition in the legislation.
We offered some suggestions and we had one amendment, which I would have preferred. Let me read that amendment to you. It appeared in Issue No. 11 at page 11:7 of the minutes of the Special Committee on a Northern Gas Pipeline. It reads:
39.1 Nothing in this Act shall be construed so as to prejudice any existing rights or interests of Indian and Native people residing in the areas traversed by the pipeline nor shall any provisions of this Act in any manner be construed as as to prejudice the negotiation of the final settlement of those Indian and Native claims.
Hon. members can compare that amendment with the amendment now before us. As I indicated I would have preferred the one which I have just quoted, for two reasons. First of all, the amendment which I presented had the word "Indian" in it. I think that is important because it specifically recognizes the rights of that group of people, and the Indians as defined under the British North America Act, Section 91(24). This section was redefined again in the Supreme Court, as I recall, in 1938 for the Inuit or Eskimo. Secondly, there is the latter part, which is very significant. Let me read it again:
... nor shall any provisions of this Act in any manner be construed so as to prejudice the negotiation of the final settlement of those Indian and Native claims.
I suggested at the time, and I suggest again, that that amendment would have been a far more preferable one. But, sir, I must emphasize that it was not possible. It was rejected by the Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council, and rejected by the government. It was important to have something in this legislation to protect in some way the rights of the Indian and native people. With the amendment that is in my name, together with a significant change that was made under clause 3(c) and which I quote:
To facilitate the efficient and expeditious planning and construction of the pipeline, taking into account local and regional interests, the interests of residents, particularly of native people, and recognizing the responsibility of the Government of Canada and other governments, it is appropriate to ensure that any native claim related to the land on which the pipeline is to be situated is to be dealt with in a just and equitable fashion.
I do believe that gives some protection and some guarantee to the Indian and native people. On the other hand I must again emphasize my disappointment that the government did not support the initial amendment, or indeed some other amendments, which would have more adequately protected the rights of the Indian and native people.
Let me conclude by quoting from the excellent brief which was presented by the National Indian Brotherhood to the

special Senate committee, I believe it was yesterday, March 21, 1978. At page 20 of the brief presented by Noel V. Starblanket, president of the National Indian Brotherhood, it states:
We respect the sovereignty of parliament. But we suggest that that too has its limits. If terms such as "a just and equitable settlement" have any real meaning, they must mean a settlement which speaks to the secure future of the Indian peoples as distinct peoples within confederation.
Sir, that should be the goal; that should be the objective of the government. I would hope that the government interprets the amendment which I have presented to the House in that fashion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to participate very briefly. I want to make a couple of comments on the two motions before us, motion No. 6 which the government intends to accept, and motion No. 4 which the government intends to reject.
I agree in part with the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) that the bill has been improved by the committee process and the number of amendments made to the bill as a result. I thought there was some very positive input from native groups, other people, and from members of parliament participating in the committee. I was very impressed with the reaction of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) and the chief spokesmen for the opposition parties in the way they addressed themselves to the native question. Most important, the special pipeline committee and the Senate committee have given the native groups ample opportunity to express their views first-hand to them. As I said, they were certainly well listened to and reacted to by the government.
In response to the committee discussions, the government has agreed to accept two important amendments, recognizing, first, the need to take account of native interests in the planning and construction of the pipeline and the responsibilities of governments to ensure that native land claims are dealt with equitably and, second, affirming that any native land claims will continue to exist notwithstanding passage of the bill.
The government gives a very high priority to the settlement of claims on the pipeline route, and has made extensive efforts to achieve this objective. Sustained negotiations were conducted during 1977, and late in the autumn both sides expressed the view that an agreement should be attainable early in 1978.
Since then, the Indians have recessed the negotiations to review and revise their position. We hope to have their new position at an early date. An agreement, by definition, requires the assent of both parties. While the government is anxious to arrive at a settlement, it cannot move more quickly than the Indians are willing to go.
I wish to respond to a point made by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent which rather surprised me. He mentioned the report to which the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) made reference at the committee stage.
March 22, 1978

It seems to me that that, if anything, will only prejudice the successful conclusion of the land claims that were engaged in, and I want to put on record what the Deputy Prime Minister said in response to that in committee. He said:
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that it is important to state that the government has absolutely no intention of legislating a settlement. Our intention is to pursue negotiations and it has been stated by myself and the minister to proceed with negotiations. If we had in mind to legislate a settlement, probably it would be in the bill.
This was further substantiated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a day or so later in the House when, on March 16, he said as reported at page 3826 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that this phrase was taken from a document prepared at a lower level of the bureaucracy, indicating various alternatives. There is no hesitation on my part in repeating what the Deputy Prime Minister said last night before the committee, that there is no intention on the part of the government to proceed in any way than by looking for a negotiated settlement. The legislation speaks for itself. It has been reported out of the committee today,
I understand, and indicates no intention to legislate.
I would hope that through you, Mr. Speaker, we can extend this conversation to the native people in the north, to convey that statement by the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister, a statement that has been made in this place and other places by a number of ministers of Indian affairs. It is a position the government subscribes to very sincerely.
I wish to respond to another point made by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent. He wished to have a much stronger amendment in place of amendment No. 6 that he has on the order paper. I suggest that one of the people he should have talked to in that regard is the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) who did not take a viewpoint which agreed entirely with that.
If you are talking about whether the government would have accepted a stronger amendment, I do not think the government would have had any difficulty accepting the original amendment which read "Nothing in this act shall operate so as to extinguish any native land claim, right, title or interest that the native people of Canada may have had prior to the coming into force of this act in and to the land on which the pipeline will be situated." This position was strongly supported and put forward by the Council of Yukon Indians last night at the pipeline hearings in the Senate.
The hon. member for Lambton-Kent might review again his comments on the second stage inquiry. With the proposal, as set out by the government, to take specific draft terms and conditions to the people in the Yukon and to the people in northern British Columbia, the native people will be in a much stronger position to be able to realize what is being proposed and to be able to react to the specifics, rather than have an open second stage inquiry which deals largely in generalities, perhaps describing problems rather than looking at the specific approaches that might be taken.
The government suggests this process will be more productive and, in the long run, more acceptable to the native people, both in the Yukon and British Columbia, than would another second stage inquiry as suggested by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent.
Northern Pipeline
1 conclude by again saying that the government intends to oppose motion No. 4 which would have left entirely in native hands the progress of the project and, indeed, the future of this bill, and by saying that we will be supporting motion No. 6.

Mr. Speaker, the speech of the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) displays his abysmal ignorance with regard to the native people in the Yukon. He stood up and informed the members of this House that native people in the Yukon do not live in the traditional fashion. I invite him to visit Old Crow where they do just that all year round. There is a whole village of people in that area in the Yukon who live in just that way, and a great many others as well. His speech was full of inaccurate statements and absolute rubbish.
We would like to have seen a stronger amendment in this bill with regard to native rights. Let me make this clear at the outset. The original bill that was presented to parliament was glaring in its omission of any native presence. It was at the insistence of this party that that native presence was inserted in the bill. The general impression that is given in the media is that it is a government thought and a government amendment. That thought and that amendment were at our initiative. That amendment was supported in committee by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas).
It is surprising that where constructive discussions could have been had, the New Democratic Party representation on that committee did not advance a single amendment during the 21 hearings. Now they have a spokesman who has not even attended a single meeting of the 21 that were held. That is one of the reasons why they are not contributing intelligent amendments at this stage and not contributing intelligent debate. They are absolutely ignorant of what went on in committee. I do not criticize the absence of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. It is a pity he is not here to straighten out his colleagues who are participating in this debate.
If it were not for the contributions made in committee by this party, we would have had no native presence in this bill. We would have had no protection for them at all. However, we do not go along with the theory advanced by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie, on behalf of this party, that there should be no development whatsoever until native claims are settled. If you take that position, you may as well kiss goodbye to a project that is going to be very significant with regard to the creation of thousands of jobs and will contribute to the growth of a steel and pipe industry in Canada which will involve thousands of positions. Is that what the NDP want?
Is it to be held up by 5,000 native people because they insist on settlement before the project goes ahead? In our view, that is not progress. Our position has always been that there is no reason why negotiated settlement cannot go hand in hand with development. If you accept the native position, there would be no new mines employing workers, no industrial development whatsoever in the Yukon until native claims are settled.
